because discrimination in our legislation flows through not just to the legal issues like certificates, but also how people treat other people. | "Unfortunately, in this case, we saw Marco treated with disrespect when he simply wanted to make arrangements for the death of somebody he loved. | Related: Briton who died on honeymoon in Australia to have same-sex marriage recognised | "The fact that David... offered his organs for donation to keep other South Australians alive and healthy - and his husband had to put up with this level of disrespect - is a disgrace." | Weatherill said he would introduce legislation to remove discrimination in South Australia and would continue to advocate for marriage equality nationally. | A bill that would recognise same-sex marriages at a federal level, introduced by the Australian Greens Senator Sarah Hanson Young in 2014, was on Thursday being debated in the Senate. | The recognition of foreign marriages bill would amend the Marriage Act 1961 to remove the prohibition of same-sex marriages solemnised in a foreign country and recognise them under Australian law. | Senator Robert Simms, the Greens spokesperson for lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex issues, said the bill would bring South Australia, Western Australia, the ACT and the Northern Territory into line with the rest of the country. | "No one should ever have to go through the trauma experienced by Marco... We have to remedy this complex web of relationship laws so married couples receive the acknowledgement they deserve. | "It is embarrassing that [South Australia], the first state in the nation to decriminalise homosexuality 40 years ago, is now lagging behind as one of the last states to remove this discrimination."
head: Death certificate cancelled for Briton whose same-sex marriage not recognised in Australia; British High Commission makes provisions to issue a consular death registration instead for David Bulmer-Rizzi as South Australian death certificate failed to recognise his UK same-sex marriage Update: SA government has not cancelled death certificate, husband says

texts: An anti-poverty charity that sold dozens of flats to a property developer without telling tenants, causing a number of evictions, potentially lost 3m in the deal by apparently disposing of the homes for below-market prices. | The Glasspool Trust, a charity set up to help poor families, faces possible investigation by the charity commission for the way it sold the 63 homes in Walthamstow, north-east London, in a secret deal late last year. | Glasspool has refused to comment or say how much it sold the homes for. However, legal documents submitted when the new owners placed six of the flats for auction last week showed these were sold by the charity on the same day in November last year for 250,000 each. | Related: Poverty charity blamed for evictions after selling up to developers | This appears a significant under-valuation for two-bedroom flats in a popular part of a London district which has in recent years seen some of the sharpest property price rises in the country. The new owners, a recently established property firm known as Butterfields E17 Ltd, named after the estate concerned, subsequently put several of the flats up for sale with estate agents with asking prices of up to 350,000. | Two of the flats, both bought by Butterfields for 250,000 on 8 November last year, were resold at the auction for 300,000 and 302,000. If all 63 properties were resold at similar prices Glasspool made a potential loss of 3.15m, or almost twice the amount of charitable grants it awarded last year. | The Labour MP for Walthamstow, Stella Creasy, says she plans to write to the charity commission to ask to look into Glasspool's actions. | "It gets murkier and murkier, the deal that was done," she said. "Clearly, there are questions to be asked about whether Glasspool acted in the interests of the people they purport to act on behalf of. | "If there is a possibility they undervalued the properties to make a quick buck in London's toxic housing market, then clearly the charity commission ought to be taking a look at this." | Under laws governing charities, trustees are obliged to ensure that any assets or property are sold for the best market price possible. In theory, they can be held personally liable for losses. | Glasspool did not tell any of the tenants, some of whom have lived in the properties for many years, that it was selling their homes. A number only learned what was happening when the new owners sent them eviction notices. | Some tenants are also questioning why the charity, set up 75 years ago with a bequest from a wealthy businessman, did not offer residents the chance to buy their homes first. | Monika Kojak, who has lived in one of the ground-floor flats for eight years, said she was appalled to learn it had most likely been sold for 250,000, a sum she and her husband could have just afforded. | "I can't honestly say what I think, I'll start swearing," she said. "It's awful. I can't understand why they've done things like that." | Glasspool had not once contacted residents to explain what happened, she added. "It's terrible. We've been with them for so many years. For me it was eight years, but some of the other residents it was 20-something years." | The charity's trustees said, via a PR agency, that they do not wish to comment on the sale prices, why they did not tell tenants, or how they selected the new owners, an Essex-based property company formed in April last year as a vehicle to buy the homes. | In its only statement so far, released earlier this month, Glasspool said it had decided to sell the 63 homes on the Butterfields estate, a pair of adjoining streets of purpose-built 1930s flats, as it was never set up as a housing provider and it wanted to maximise the amount of grants it gives, which mainly go to provide households goods such as fridges. | The charity said it was "very saddened" to learn tenants were being evicted and that during the sale it sought assurances from their selling agents about this. A spokesman for Butterfields E17 has said the company was never asked about this. Butterfields says it plans to evict more of the tenants as it gradually sells the flats. | None of the trustees contacted individually responded to requests for comment. The trustees include a retired oil industry executive, a social worker and a civil servant who also runs her own property-letting business.
head: Poverty charity may have lost 3m by selling flats below market value; Glasspool Trust, which sold dozens of flats in Walthamstow to developers without telling tenants, may face investigation over secret deal

texts: Donald Trump has told a crowd of 7,500 that he was holding back during the first presidential debate with Hillary Clinton because he did not want to embarrass her. | He insisted that every poll showed him winning the debates but cited only internet surveys to prove this; every scientific poll taken in the aftermath of the debate showed a majority of viewers believing the Democratic nominee had won. | Related: Consensus: Clinton wins debate - but Trump is far from finished | The Republican nominee's unhappiness with coverage of his widely panned performance showed. Three times in the course of a rally in Florida, Trump called out "the corrupt corporate media" and gestured towards his supporters to turn towards the press pen to boo, hiss and even, in one instance, shout "go to hell". | Trump constantly revisited different moments in the debate and told of how, before taking the stage, "I took a deep breath and pretended I was talking to my family." He recounted what he felt were his best lines during the debate - like, "You are experienced but it's bad experience" - and touted how he had done well on the issue of trade and exposed Clinton's "real positions" on Nafta, which he described as "the single worst deal you'll ever see". | He even criticised Lester Holt, the debate moderator, whom Trump described as "the emcee", for challenging him when he praised stop and frisk, a controversial police tactic that involved New York police officers stopping pedestrians without a warrant, asking them questions and checking them for weapons. A federal judge ruled in 2013 that the practice was unconstitutional as it disproportionately targeted African Americans and Latinos. Trump insisted: "I also explained last night stop and frisk was constitutional. The emcee argued with me, taking up the time. Law enforcement does stop and frisk every day." | Trump also re-litigated his false claim that he had opposed the Iraq war from the beginning, asking the crowd for approval. "And does everybody believe me, I was against going into Iraq?" he asked the crowd. | In contrast, Clinton took a far more jubilant tone on Tuesday, mocking Trump's complaints about his microphone. "Anybody who complained about the microphone is not having a good night," she told reporters on her plane. | Though Trump supporters in Florida responded with loud cheers when asked by state party chair Blaise Ingoglia who they thought won the debate, they were far more equivocal in one-on-one interviews. | Standing outside the rally, Monty and Cat Alger, an ex-husband and ex-wife, thought Trump had room for improvement. Monty Alger thought Trump "could have done better", but said he despised Clinton: "If it were up to me, I'd put her ass in jail." | Cat Alger echoed a famous country music song: "Like Tammy [Wynette], stand by your man." She supported the Republican nominee because "he tells it like it is, whether you want to hear it or not". | Matty Hall, from Palm Bay, Florida, said she felt that "for it being [Trump's] first debate and no experience, he did better than I thought". However, she was disappointed by the lack of discussion of issues she thought were important in the debate like "security, keeping our border safe and work". | Even Jeff Bellinger, from Melbourne, Florida, thought "it could have been better". He thought that "it wasn't [Trump]'s worst debate but it wasn't his best". Bellinger added that he saw "a few different times Trump could have capitalized but it didn't make any difference to me". | Grace Owens of Brunswick, Georgia, wearing a hat that read "deplorable" in cursive script and a T-shirt that proclaimed America First, thought neither candidate won the debate. In her analysis, Trump "needed to come out and hit her harder than he did." She added: "He did OK but Trump can do better". | Owens took issue at those who might take offense at her shirt. Before Trump, the slogan America First had been associated with those wanting to keep the United States out of the second world war, many of whom were sympathetic to Nazi Germany. In her opinion, "they are just looking to attack Trump. Screw them."
head: Donald Trump boasts after first debate against Clinton: 'I didn't want to embarrass her'; Insisting every poll showed him as the winner, Republican nominee blasts 'corrupt media' and recounts what he felt were his best lines

texts: The beleaguered French president, Fran ois Hollande, has appeared on a primetime TV show, promising life in France was "getting better" as he took questions from French voters in a risky bid to improve his dire poll ratings a year before the 2017 presidential race. | The Socialist French president has slumped so low in the polls that he is now the country's least popular head of state on record. He is increasingly rejected not just by the right, but also overwhelmingly on the left. An Odoxa poll in Le Parisien on Thursday found 76% of French people think he should abandon the idea of running for a second term in office. Different polls this month show that between 13% and 20% of voters have a favourable view of him. | In a 90-minute programme, Hollande insisted: "My policies are producing results and will produce even more." Despite a suggestion by Emmanuel Macron, the economy minister and possible presidential challenger, that part of the reform programme had been halted in the run-up to the presidential election, Hollande said he would continue reforms in his last year in office, "every day, until the very last day of my mandate". | Macron recently launched his own political movement, fuelling speculation about his ambitions, but Hollande attempted to put him in his place, stressing his own presidential "authority" and saying Macron, his one-time adviser, "knows what he owes me". | Hollande insisted: "Things are going better: there is more growth, less deficit, more competitiveness, better margins for companies, more purchasing power for workers." But he was repeatedly asked about the rising mass unemployment that has plagued his term in office. Using the show to try to reach out to disappointed voters on the left, Hollande stressed he would protect workers' rights. Hollande said he would make a decision at the end of this year on whether to run again for office in 2017. He also ruled out a ban on Muslim headscarves at universities, which his prime minister, Manuel Valls, called for earlier this week. | Hollande is not only in trouble over France's economic stagnation and stubbornly high unemployment of about 10%, which continues to rise in France while it falls in other large European economies. He is also grappling with his own personal public relations disaster over contested labour reforms that have brought students onto the streets. As part of a broader street protest movement, Nuit debout - which loosely means Rise Up at Night - disappointed people on the left have occupied city squares at night to debate the future of society. | Hollande's Socialist party is bitterly divided, and voters accuse him of zig-zagging on stop-start reforms that are seen by some as not going far enough and by others as betraying his promise four years ago that his main adversary was the world of finance. His poll ratings briefly rose after last year's terrorist attacks on Paris before falling again - but even on terrorism, he recently had to make a damaging climbdown after failing to get support from both houses of parliament over his plans to strip French citizenship from convicted terrorists. | There are now doubts among some on the broader left about whether Hollande could run again for a second presidential term next year, and some are agitating for a primary race to choose a candidate. Hollande has said he won't run again unless he can stem the rise of unemployment - which still looks tricky. However, his entourage are briefing that he is optimistic about running again. | After student protests over labour reforms, the government this week announced about half a billion euros in aid for students in an attempt to defuse anger from French youth. But it is not certain that the measures - after which Hollande was dubbed "Father Christmas" - will calm the mood of distrust. When he was elected four years ago, Hollande asked to be judged only on whether the lives of young people improved during his presidency, but this issue is fraught. | The 2017 French presidential race is at this point impossible to predict. It is more open than any contest for decades, because the key contenders are not yet known. | For the first time, the right is having a primary race to choose its candidate in November, with the political veteran and one-time prime minister Alain Jupp still the surprise frontrunner, but Nicolas Sarkozy is hoping for a return to the Elys e palace, and several other contenders are promising to overhaul the right. | There have been calls for a broader primary on the left but this is uncertain. The hard-left firebrand Jean-Luc M lenchon has announced his candidacy, which could eat into a portion of the leftwing vote. The Front National's Marine Le Pen has consistently been tipped by polls as capable of knocking out a mainstream candidate to reach the final round run-off.
head: Fran ois Hollande faces TV grilling from voters; French president defends his record a year before 2017 election as poll finds most people believe he should not run again

texts: San Francisco police officers shot and killed a 27-year-old black woman near the city's Bayview neighborhood on Thursday morning, authorities said. | The woman, who has not been identified, was allegedly in a stolen car when she was approached by two uniformed officers. The woman "did not comply originally with the investigation" and drove off, then quickly crashed the car, police chief Greg Suhr said at the scene of the shooting. | Related: San Francisco's liberal image marred by scandal-prone police department | One of the officers, a sergeant, fired a single shot at the woman, striking her. The officers immediately removed the woman from her car and administered CPR, Suhr said. | The woman was transported to the hospital, where she died. | "This is exactly the kind of thing, with all of our reforms, that we're trying to avoid," Suhr told reporters. | The chief did not state whether or not the woman was armed. | The shooting comes amid a string of controversial shootings and scandals for the San Francisco Police Department. | It took place less than two miles from where a group of police shot and killed Mario Woods, a 26-year-old black man, in a barrage of gunfire on 2 December 2015. Bystander video of the shooting contradicted police statements that Wood, who was carrying a knife, extended his arm toward police prior to their opening fire. | The neighborhood, known as the Bayview, is one of the only remaining black neighborhoods in San Francisco, a city whose black population has fallen to less than 6%. | In April, police shot and killed Luis Gongora, a homeless man who they claimed had charged at the officers with a knife. Numerous eye witnesses challenged the police version of the incident, which surveillance footage showed unfolded in just 30 seconds. | Since 2015, the department has also been forced to reveal two separate batches of racist and homophobic text messages exchanged between groups of officers, forcing prosecutors to reexamine thousands of criminal cases. | The department is currently under a voluntary review by the Department of Justice's office of community oriented policing services. | Four of the city's eleven supervisors have called for chief Suhr to resign. | If you have information about this shooting, please contact julia.wong@theguardian.com
head: San Francisco police fatally shoot black woman in city's Bayview neighborhood; The unidentified 27-year-old, allegedly in a stolen car, was shot and killed less than two miles from where Mario Woods was killed by officers in 2015
